Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How much does public transport cost in Sweden?
Answer: I can offer an example from the world of train commuters in the countryside, reflecting prices as of mid-2022. My train ticket is a monthly one I buy for about 2500 Swedish Crowns. With it, I get unlimited train travel between my village and the city where I work. It’s 150 kilometers each way, and if I go in five times a week, that works out to a cost of about 65 Swedish Crowns each way, which is about the cost of three liters of gasoline - but there is no car out there that could cover the distance on that. And it’s a two hour trip, which a train traveler can spend sleeping or surfing the internet. I go in on average three times a week throughout the academic year, so my theoretical price tag of each trip is more like about 100 Swedish Crowns each way. That would correspond with the fuel cost of my Toyota Prius for the same distance. If I were to buy a single ticket each way for the same trip, its cost would be 250 Swedish Crowns each way (about 25 US Dollars as of June 2022). These tickets can be tax deductible from a certain, annual expenditure upward, so it’s really not all that scary.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What is a reasonable temperature for a house in winter at night?
Answer: It would depend a little on humidity levels, too. In my experience, the drier the air, the lower you can set your thermostat without being uncomfortable. I live in a subarctic climate that is quite dry, and the default temperature my house is kept at is 18 degrees Celsius. That’s 64.4 Fahrenheit. When I tell my friends in England or New Jersey, they are like “whaaat?? That’s freezing!!” But no. It’s not. I sit there in shorts and t-shirt, barefoot. Not because I’m a polar bear, but because it actually feels very nice. From living in England and New Jersey, I remember that I used to set my thermostat to higher settings there, too. The humidity is, after all, water molecules in the air, which have a cooling effect. Get rid of them, maybe by running a heat pump instead of a water filled or oil filled radiator, and you can benefit of the low humidity savings, too. I have tried setting things to 20 and even 22 Celsius at my house here, but it was simply a waste of energy. Do any activity at all, and you break into a sweat. One thing though, before you get all enthusiastic and try it with minimal temperature settings now: Keep it above 16 Celsius to avoid the accumulation of mold. Granted, in a dry climate, that danger is minimal, but once it takes hold, you’re stuck with it.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is it hard to adapt to Swedish culture?
Answer: It depends a lot on your starting point. Swedish culture is all about seeking consensus and avoiding conflict while respecting the individual and following scientific, rather than ideological values. Fiercely egalitarian, attuned to environmental friendliness, and trusting in the good in people. Someone from an authoritarian, conflict glorifying macho culture who goes it alone every time and likes to follow doctrine would be quite outcast here. Other than that, Swedish culture is also about enjoying nature and the seasons, seeking solitude, taking it mellow, retreating to one's own space, and taking a time out to play. If that's not you, well… at least you know where you'd stand. My observation has been that those who find it easiest to blend in here are usually Dutch, British, Norwegian, Danish, Finnish, French, Canadian, and Australian. Also fairly good fits seem to be Czechs, Poles, Austrians, Belgians, and those from the Baltic states.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Are German people willing to suffer from the cold in winter at the cost of not buying Russian natural gas?
Answer: If I actually lived in Germany now, and had gas central heating, the simple answer would be: No more gas for me. I can’t pay for it anyway, at these rates, and even if I could, I wouldn’t want it. What’s the alternative? Electricity. Convection heaters are pretty much sold out even now, in the hottest, most scorching summer Germany has ever recorded, I am told. People are showing quite clearly with these purchases what they think of Russian gas.

Question: Why are we passing from the world?
Answer: I believe we pass on because we have some place better to be. We are not meant to stay here. Just look at how we change - life is meant to end some day. Everything in this world has an expiry date. It’s like with cars. You get a new one, you drive it, it ages, and eventually breaks down irreparably. The driver gets out and, well, who knows. Do we get a “new car”? Are we done driving for good? We don’t know. But the driver doesn’t get scrapped with the car.
